note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How much of the world's ocean is inside a marine protected area?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 8.4% — against a target of 30% by 2030. More than nine tenths of the ocean has no protection at all.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Vastly too high.
questions.action: Find the nearest marine protected area to your coast.

questions.prompt: The world's target for ocean protection by 2030 is:
questions.whyCorrect: 30% — meaning protection must more than triple in under five years, from today's 8.4%.
whyWrong: That's the current level, not the target.
Total protection is not the goal.
questions.action: Ask what activities a marine protected area restricts.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's fish stocks are overfished?
questions.whyCorrect: 35.5% — over a third are caught faster than they can reproduce, and that share grows about 1% every year.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high — about two thirds remain sustainable.
questions.action: Look up whether the fish you eat is overfished.

questions.prompt: What share of fish stocks are still fished sustainably?
questions.whyCorrect: 64.5% as of 2021 — down from 62.3% by earlier measures, and shrinking about a percentage point a year.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — about two thirds are sustainable.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask what 'biologically sustainable' means for a fish stock.

questions.prompt: The overfished share of stocks is changing by roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: Growing about 1% a year. Slow, steady, and cumulative — this is how a resource gets used up without anyone noticing a single dramatic moment.
whyWrong: The trend is toward more overfishing, not less.
There is a consistent yearly deterioration.
questions.action: Project 35.5% forward ten years at 1% a year.

questions.prompt: How much fish is caught illegally or unreported each year?
questions.whyCorrect: Up to 26 million tons — about 15% of all fish caught worldwide, taken outside any rules or quotas.
whyWrong: Illegal fishing is a massive global industry.
A thousand times too low.
questions.action: Look up how a fishing boat can be tracked by satellite.

questions.prompt: Illegal and unreported fishing is roughly what share of all catches?
questions.whyCorrect: About 15% — one fish in seven is caught outside the law. It undercuts legal fishers and makes stocks impossible to manage.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high, though the real figure is severe.
questions.action: Ask how you'd know if a fish was caught legally.

questions.prompt: How much of the excess heat from greenhouse gases does the ocean absorb?
questions.whyCorrect: 90%. The ocean has been shielding us from the full force of warming — and that heat does not disappear, it accumulates.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Ask where the heat would have gone without the ocean.

questions.prompt: Ocean heat content in 2024 was:
options: The highest in 65 years of records
questions.whyCorrect: The highest ever measured, and the rate of ocean warming has doubled since 2005. The ocean's heat uptake is accelerating.
whyWrong: Ocean heat hit a record high.
It was a record, not a typical year.
questions.action: Look up the sea temperature near you this summer.

questions.prompt: The rate of ocean warming compared with 2005 is:
questions.whyCorrect: It has doubled since 2005 — the ocean is not just warm, it is warming faster each decade.
whyWrong: Warming accelerated, it did not slow.
The rate has changed substantially.
questions.action: Ask what happens to sea level as water warms.

questions.prompt: Ocean pH has fallen from 8.1 in 1985 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 8.04 — a small-looking number that means the ocean is measurably more acidic, dissolving the shells of the creatures at the base of the food web.
whyWrong: That's neutral — the ocean is still alkaline.
The ocean is becoming more acidic, not less.
questions.action: Look up how the pH scale works.

questions.prompt: Ocean acidity is increasing by how much per decade?
questions.whyCorrect: -0.017 units per decade. Because pH is a logarithmic scale, that small number represents a substantial chemical change.
whyWrong: A hundred times too large.
Acidity is rising as the ocean absorbs CO2.
questions.action: Ask why a logarithmic scale makes small numbers big.

questions.prompt: What share of coral reefs experienced bleaching heat stress between 2023 and 2025?
questions.whyCorrect: 84% — the most widespread bleaching event ever recorded, hitting reefs in 83 countries and territories.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Far below the actual extent.
questions.action: Look up what a bleached coral looks like.

questions.prompt: Coral bleaching between 2023 and 2025 hit reefs in how many countries?
questions.whyCorrect: 83 countries and territories — essentially every reef nation on Earth, at the same time.
whyWrong: More than have coral reefs.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Find three countries with major coral reefs.

questions.prompt: What share of coral species face extinction?
questions.whyCorrect: 44% — nearly half. Reefs cover under 1% of the ocean floor but support around a quarter of all marine species.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high, though the real figure is grave.
questions.action: Look up how many species depend on coral reefs.

questions.prompt: How much coral cover did the world lose between 2009 and 2018?
questions.whyCorrect: 14% of all coral — roughly the reef area of Australia's entire Great Barrier Reef, gone in under a decade.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
That's the share of species facing extinction.
questions.action: Ask what depends on a reef besides fish.

questions.prompt: What share of marine key biodiversity areas are protected?
questions.whyCorrect: 46% — far better than the 8.4% overall ocean figure. Protection is being targeted where it matters most, but over half these critical areas remain unprotected.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
That's total ocean protection, not key areas.
questions.action: Ask what makes an area 'key' for biodiversity.

questions.prompt: How many countries are working on marine spatial planning?
questions.whyCorrect: 126 countries as of 2023, a 20% rise in a year — though only 45 have formally approved a plan.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
More countries than are engaged.
questions.action: Ask what competing uses a sea area has.

questions.prompt: Of 126 countries working on marine spatial plans, how many have formally approved one?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 45. Starting a plan is much easier than agreeing one, because it means telling industries where they cannot go.
whyWrong: That's the number engaged, not approved.
Far more than five have approved plans.
questions.action: Ask why an approved plan is harder than a draft.

questions.prompt: Ocean acidification monitoring stations have grown from 178 in 2021 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 765 by 2025 — more than quadrupled in four years. The world is finally measuring what it has long been changing.
whyWrong: The growth was far larger.
Stations increased, not decreased.
questions.action: Ask why measuring comes before fixing.

questions.prompt: What share of fish landed comes from sustainably fished stocks?
questions.whyCorrect: 77.2% of landings — higher than the 64.5% of stocks, because the big, well-managed stocks produce the most fish.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
Far too pessimistic.
questions.action: Ask why 'share of stocks' differs from 'share of fish'.

questions.prompt: Countries scoring highest on anti-illegal-fishing measures rose from 48% to:
questions.whyCorrect: 56% between 2018 and 2024, with the overall implementation rating rising from 3 to 4. Enforcement is genuinely improving.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
The share rose, it did not fall.
questions.action: Look up what a port state inspection does.

questions.prompt: Ocean acidification happens because:
options: Acid rain falls into the sea
The ocean absorbs CO2, which forms carbonic acid in water
questions.whyCorrect: Dissolved CO2 reacts with seawater to form carbonic acid. That's why acidification tracks emissions almost exactly.
whyWrong: Acid rain is a separate, largely solved problem.
Biological waste is not the driver.
questions.action: Try dissolving CO2 in water and testing the pH.

questions.prompt: Acidification most directly threatens creatures that:
options: Build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate
questions.whyCorrect: More acidic water dissolves calcium carbonate — so oysters, corals, and the tiny plankton at the base of the whole food web struggle to build.
whyWrong: Speed offers no protection from chemistry.
Acidification is an ocean process.
questions.action: Put a seashell in vinegar and watch what happens.

questions.prompt: Coral bleaching happens when:
options: Heat stress makes coral expel the algae that feed and colour it
questions.whyCorrect: Corals live with algae inside them. Under heat stress they eject the algae, turning white and starving — recoverable if the heat passes soon enough.
whyWrong: Bleaching is a biological stress response.
Heat, not cold, is the main trigger.
questions.action: Look up before-and-after photos of a bleached reef.

questions.prompt: The ocean absorbing 90% of excess heat means:
options: The air would be far hotter without it
questions.whyCorrect: Without the ocean's heat uptake, surface warming would be dramatically worse — but the ocean is paying for it in heatwaves, bleaching and rising seas.
whyWrong: Ocean heat content hit a 65-year record in 2024.
Both ocean and air continue to warm.
questions.action: Ask what a 'marine heatwave' does to fish.

questions.prompt: Going from 8.4% to 30% ocean protection by 2030 requires:
options: More than tripling protected ocean in under five years
questions.whyCorrect: Protection must more than triple, mostly in the high seas beyond any country's control — which is why a new high seas treaty matters so much.
whyWrong: The required change is enormous.
The current trajectory falls far short.
questions.action: Look up who governs the ocean beyond national waters.

questions.prompt: 26 million tons of illegal fishing harms legal fishers because:
options: It floods markets with untaxed fish and empties the stocks they depend on
questions.whyCorrect: Illegal operators ignore quotas and costs, undercut prices, and deplete the same stocks legal fishers rely on next season.
whyWrong: It directly undercuts legal operations.
The harm is economic and ecological, not culinary.
questions.action: Ask how a supermarket verifies its fish supply.

questions.prompt: Marine spatial planning means:
options: Deciding which parts of the sea are used for fishing, shipping, energy or protection
questions.whyCorrect: It's zoning for the ocean — resolving conflicts between fishing fleets, shipping lanes, wind farms and protected habitat before they collide.
whyWrong: Mapping is one input, not the plan itself.
It concerns ocean space, not outer space.
questions.action: List four different uses of the sea near you.

questions.prompt: 84% of reefs bleached in a single event tells us:
options: Bleaching is now a global synchronised event, not a local one
questions.whyCorrect: Local reefs used to bleach in bad years. Now ocean heat is high enough to bleach almost every reef on Earth simultaneously.
whyWrong: It was the most widespread bleaching ever recorded.
83 countries were affected.
questions.action: Ask what makes an event 'global' rather than local.

questions.prompt: The 30x30 ocean target refers to:
questions.whyCorrect: 30% protected by 2030 — from today's 8.4%. It's the headline commitment of global biodiversity policy for the sea.
whyWrong: Not a measure of fish density.
It concerns area, not depth.
questions.action: Ask what your country has committed to protecting.

questions.prompt: Ocean pH dropping from 8.1 to 8.04 represents an acidity increase of roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: Because pH is logarithmic, a 0.06-unit drop means roughly 15% more hydrogen ions — a large chemical shift hidden in a small-looking number.
whyWrong: The change is chemically substantial.
That confuses the pH difference with a percentage.
questions.action: Look up why each pH unit is a tenfold change.

questions.prompt: Marine key biodiversity area protection at 46% versus total ocean protection at 8.4% shows:
options: Protection is being concentrated where biodiversity is richest
questions.whyCorrect: Conservation is targeting the highest-value habitat first — a sensible strategy, but 54% of critical areas still have no protection.
whyWrong: Both figures measure different things correctly.
Key areas get far more protection than average.
questions.action: Ask how you'd choose which sea area to protect first.

questions.prompt: Coral reefs cover under 1% of the seafloor but support roughly:
options: A quarter of all marine species
questions.whyCorrect: About a quarter of all marine life depends on reefs at some point — which is why 44% of coral species facing extinction matters far beyond coral.
whyWrong: Reefs are vastly more biodiverse than their area suggests.
Reefs are among the richest habitats on Earth.
questions.action: Look up how many fish species live on one reef.

questions.prompt: Ocean acidification monitoring quadrupling to 765 stations matters because:
options: You can't manage or negotiate about what you can't measure
questions.whyCorrect: Better data makes acidification visible in policy debates — and reveals where shellfish industries and reefs are most at risk.
whyWrong: Measurement is the foundation of any response.
Monitoring records change; it doesn't prevent it.
questions.action: Find out if there's an ocean monitoring station near you.

questions.prompt: Sustainable stocks fell from 62.3% by earlier measures to 64.5% by newer ones. This mainly reflects:
options: Improved assessment methods, not a real reversal of the downward trend
questions.whyCorrect: Better methods revised the estimate slightly upward, but the underlying trend — about 1% more overfished each year — continues.
whyWrong: The overall trend remains negative.
Both estimates are valid under their own methods.
questions.action: Ask why revised statistics aren't the same as real change.

questions.prompt: The anti-illegal-fishing implementation rating rose from 3 to 4 between 2018 and 2024. That means:
options: Countries are measurably better at implementing international fishing rules
questions.whyCorrect: A full point improvement on the scale, with the top-scoring group growing from 48% to 56% of countries — real, if partial, progress.
whyWrong: The score improved.
There was a measurable rise.
questions.action: Ask what makes a country good at enforcing fishing rules.

questions.prompt: The ocean has absorbed 90% of excess heat AND large amounts of CO2. Together this means:
options: The ocean is both hotter and more acidic
questions.whyCorrect: Two separate consequences of the same emissions — heat that bleaches reefs, and acid that dissolves shells. Marine life faces both at once.
whyWrong: Both heat content and pH have changed measurably.
pH fell from 8.1 to 8.04 as well.
questions.action: Name one species harmed by heat and one by acidity.

questions.prompt: Only 45 countries have approved marine spatial plans. The main obstacle is:
options: Agreeing a plan means restricting where powerful industries can operate
questions.whyCorrect: Planning is technical; approving is political. Every zone drawn tells fishing fleets, shipping firms or energy companies where they cannot go.
whyWrong: Mapping technology is widely available.
126 countries have started the process.
questions.action: Ask who would object to a new protected area near you.

questions.prompt: 77.2% of landings are sustainable but only 64.5% of stocks are. This means:
options: Large, well-managed stocks produce most of the catch
questions.whyCorrect: A few big, carefully managed stocks supply most of the world's fish, while many smaller stocks — harder to monitor — are the overfished ones.
whyWrong: Illegal catch is about 15%.
They measure different things and are both consistent.
questions.action: Ask why big fisheries are easier to manage than small ones.

questions.prompt: The ocean's warming rate doubling since 2005 means:
options: The ocean absorbs heat faster each decade, with less buffering capacity ahead
questions.whyCorrect: Faster ocean warming means faster sea level rise, more marine heatwaves, and less of a buffer protecting the atmosphere.
whyWrong: Ocean heat content is rising.
2024 set a 65-year record for ocean heat.
questions.action: Look up what a marine heatwave did to one fishery.

questions.prompt: 26 million tons of illegal fishing compares with total global catch as roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: About 15%, or one fish in seven, caught outside any legal framework — invisible to the science that sets sustainable quotas.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Most fishing is legal and reported.
questions.action: Ask how quotas can work when 15% goes uncounted.

questions.prompt: Marine spatial planning participation rose 20% in a single year to 126 countries. This suggests:
options: Ocean planning is gaining momentum, even if approvals lag
questions.whyCorrect: A 20% jump in engagement in one year is fast for international policy — the bottleneck is approval, not interest.
whyWrong: Participation grew substantially.
Only 45 plans have been approved.
questions.action: Ask what turns a plan into a law.

questions.prompt: 44% of coral species facing extinction matters to people because reefs:
options: Feed hundreds of millions and shield coasts from storm waves
questions.whyCorrect: Reefs supply food and income to hundreds of millions and act as natural breakwaters. Losing them means losing both protein and coastal defence.
whyWrong: Reefs provide food, income and physical protection.
Reef fisheries and tourism are economically enormous.
questions.action: Look up what a reef does during a storm surge.

questions.prompt: Which Goal 14 indicator is furthest from its target?
options: Ocean protection at 8.4% against a 30% target
questions.whyCorrect: Protection must more than triple in five years. Monitoring quadrupled and enforcement scores rose — protection is the laggard.
whyWrong: Stations quadrupled from 178 to 765.
Ratings improved from 3 to 4.
questions.action: Ask what makes protecting ocean harder than protecting land.

questions.prompt: Overfishing grows about 1% a year. From 35.5% today, by 2035 it would reach roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: Around 45% — nearly half of all stocks overfished within a decade if nothing changes. Slow trends compound.
whyWrong: The trend is upward without intervention.
That's a single year's change.
questions.action: Add 1% per year to 35.5% for ten years.

questions.prompt: Coral cover fell 14% between 2009 and 2018, before the 2023-25 bleaching. That suggests:
options: The recent bleaching hit reefs already weakened by a decade of loss
questions.whyCorrect: Repeated stress leaves less time to recover between events — which is why the 2023–25 event, hitting 84% of reefs, is so serious.
whyWrong: Both trends point to decline.
A seventh of coral cover was already lost.
questions.action: Ask how long a bleached reef needs to recover.

questions.prompt: A marine protected area works best when it:
options: Is actually enforced, so fish populations recover and spill over into fishing grounds
questions.whyCorrect: Well-enforced reserves let fish grow bigger and breed more, and the surplus spills into surrounding waters — which is why fishers often end up supporting them.
whyWrong: Unenforced 'paper parks' deliver little.
Most protected areas allow some regulated uses.
questions.action: Look up a fishery that recovered after a reserve was created.

questions.prompt: The ocean's role in the climate system is best described as:
options: The planet's main heat and carbon sink, absorbing 90% of excess heat
questions.whyCorrect: The ocean has quietly absorbed most of the heat and much of the carbon from emissions — which is why its chemistry and temperature are changing so fast.
whyWrong: It is the single largest component of the climate system.
It absorbs heat rather than generating it.
questions.action: Ask what would happen if the ocean stopped absorbing heat.

questions.prompt: The starkest Goal 14 fact is:
options: 84% of coral reefs bleached while only 8.4% of the ocean is protected
questions.whyCorrect: Reefs are bleaching almost everywhere while protection covers under a tenth of the sea — the scale of damage far outruns the scale of response.
whyWrong: Growing engagement is positive news.
That's a genuine improvement from 178.
questions.action: Find one thing your household could change about seafood.
